corrected_value.title: Career mobility, job match, and overeducation

prior_decision.quote: In Section 4.3, we extend Robst’s (1995) test for robustness by using an objective, as well as a subjective, measure of training participation. Both measures confirm Robst’s findings that overeducated (undereducated) workers indeed receive less (more) training than correctly allocated ones.
prior_decision.location: Section 1 (Introduction), p. 3, lines 190-198; Section 4.3, pp. 16-17, lines 864-920
prior_decision.reason: Omitted target in shipped data. Beyond citing Robst (1995) as background, the paper explicitly re-tests Robst's (1995) empirical finding on training participation in Section 4.3 (Tables 5 and 6) using the same subjective survey question in the German GSOEP sample as well as an objective formal training indicator, concluding that both measures confirm Robst's findings.

luna_triage.reason: Section 4.3 reuses the same subjective training question as Robst and adds an objective formal-training measure, then reports that overeducated workers have less training and undereducated workers more, confirming the comparison. The supplied shipped original is Sicherman (1991), a different paper and occupational-mobility finding.
luna_triage.location: Section 4.3, pp. 16-17; prior adjudication confirms omitted target
luna_triage.omission_quote: Robst (1995) used the same question and concluded for the United States that, contrary to the career mobility hypothesis, overeducated workers are no more likely to acquire knowledge that could lead to a better job. Second, we use information gathered in the years 1989 and 1993 on whether GSOEP respondents had participated in a job-related training measure lasting more than one day in the preceding three-year period (“yes” or “no”).
luna_triage.identity_quote: Both measures confirm Robst’s findings that overeducated (undereducated) workers indeed receive less (more) training than correctly allocated ones.
